chapters.title: Chapter 1: Two Families of Assets, One Question

lessons.title: The Risk-Return Trade-Off, Revisited for Alternatives

children.text: Vikram, a 41-year-old consultant in Gurugram, gets a message from his wealth manager: "Private credit fund. Target 14% a year. Volatility far lower than the Nifty. Better returns with less risk." Every investing textbook says higher return needs higher risk. So either this fund has found a free lunch, or the risk is still there and simply is not showing up in the number he was shown. This lesson shows you where that risk hides and how to do the rough math yourself.

body.text: Extra return is never free. With alternatives, you still pay for it in risk, just in currencies a volatility number does not measure: lock-ins, defaults, concentration and dependence on one manager.

children.text: The Classic Trade-Off in One Picture

Line up traditional Indian assets by the return you can reasonably expect over long periods and you get a staircase. Each step up pays more because the asset asks you to accept more uncertainty along the way.

body.title: Illustrative long-run annual return expectations, traditional assets (%)

markDefs.definition: A statistical measure of how widely an asset's returns swing around their average. Higher standard deviation means a bumpier ride.

children.text: For listed assets, the usual yardstick for "risk" on that staircase is volatility, measured as the
standard deviation
of returns. It works reasonably well for the Nifty because the Nifty has a real price every trading day. Every fall is visible, measured and included.

body.label: Nifty 50 fall, January to March 2020
body.context: Peak to trough on a closing basis during the Covid crash. Every rupee of that fall showed up in index fund NAVs in real time.

children.text: Why the Staircase Bends for Alternatives

In March 2020, nobody marked down the value of a Gurugram flat by 38%. Private credit funds and real estate funds did not report 38% falls either. Their holdings are valued by appraisal, often quarterly, so the shock arrived late, arrived smoothed, or never showed up in the reported figure at all.

Put such an asset on the staircase using its reported volatility and it looks like it sits above the line: more return for less risk. That is not a free lunch. It is a measuring problem. The risks that matter most in alternatives are simply not the kind that standard deviation captures.

body.caption: Risks a volatility number misses
headers: What it looks like in practice

cells: You cannot sell when you need the money, or can sell only at a steep discount
Flats, PE and VC funds, fractional ownership
A borrower stops paying and you recover only part of your money, years later
P2P loans, private credit, unlisted NCDs
One project, one tenant or one startup decides most of your outcome
Poor deal selection, weak controls or outright fraud
Borrowing inside the structure magnifies losses when things go wrong
Leveraged real estate, some Category III AIFs

body.text: A low volatility figure on a factsheet or platform dashboard is not evidence of low risk when the underlying prices are appraised. Before you accept it, ask two questions: how often are the holdings valued, and who does the valuing?

children.text: A Traditional Wrapper Is No Guarantee Either

Hidden risk is not only an alternatives problem. When a traditional product reaches for alternative-style returns, it takes on alternative-style risks too. India learned this with Franklin Templeton's credit-oriented debt funds, which held higher-yielding, lower-rated and thinly traded corporate paper. Their NAVs looked steady for years, right up until investors could not get their money out.

children.text: Doing the Rough Math on a High-Yield Promise

markDefs.definition: The chance, usually expressed per year, that a borrower fails to pay interest or principal as agreed.
The share of the money lent that is lost once a borrower defaults, after whatever is recovered. If you recover 60%, loss given default is 40%.

children.text: For any lending-style alternative, a headline yield is the best case. To get closer to what you might actually earn, subtract the losses you should expect from defaults and the fees you will definitely pay. Expected losses depend on two things: the
probability of default
(PD) and the
loss given default
(LGD).

body.caption: Both inputs expressed as percentages per year

body.latex: \text{Expected net return} \approx \text{Gross yield} - \text{Expected credit loss} - \text{Fees and costs}
body.caption: A rough, pre-tax estimate, not a precise forecast

children.text: Apply it to Vikram's fund. Assume a 14% gross yield, a 5% yearly chance that any given borrower defaults, 60% recovered when that happens (so LGD is 40%), and 2% a year in fees and costs.
Expected credit loss:
Expected net return:
14% − 2% − 2% = 10% a year, before tax.
Compare with a liquid alternative:
a listed AA-rated corporate bond yielding about 8.5%, which he can sell on an exchange.

The real pickup is about 1.5 percentage points, not 5.5. For that, Vikram accepts a multi-year lock-in, a portfolio of perhaps 10 to 15 loans, and the chance that defaults turn out worse than 5%. That might still be a fair trade. But it is a trade, and now he can see its price.
Credit losses cluster in bad years. Here is the same fund if a downturn doubles the default rate and recoveries fall to 40%.

content.caption: Private credit fund: base case vs stress case (illustrative)

children.text: In the stress case the fund earns less than the 8.5% AA bond, and Vikram's money is still locked in. This is the shape of alternative risk: a modest extra return in normal years, and a worse outcome with no exit in bad ones.

body.title: What does a 12% P2P yield really pay?
body.prompt: A P2P lending platform advertises a 12% average yield. Assume a 4% yearly default rate, 25% recovered on defaulted loans, and a 1% platform fee. Using the formulas above, what is the expected net return before tax, in percent?
body.explanation: LGD is 100% − 25% = 75%. Expected credit loss is 4% × 75% = 3%. Expected net return is 12% − 3% − 1% = 8%. That is barely above a bank FD, for money that can only come back as borrowers repay.

body.title: Complete the formula
body.textWithBlank: Expected credit loss equals the probability of default multiplied by the ___.
body.explanation: A high default rate with strong recoveries can cost less than a lower default rate with almost nothing recovered. You need both numbers.

children.text: Where an Alternative's Extra Return Really Comes From

markDefs.definition: The extra return investors demand for holding an asset they cannot easily sell. Chapter 2 covers it in detail.

children.text: A useful habit is to break any target return into its sources. Take a hypothetical mid-market private equity fund in India targeting 16% a year before fees. Most of that is simply equity market return, since it owns companies. Some is the
illiquidity premium
for tying up money for years. Only the remainder is genuine manager skill.

body.title: Illustrative sources of a 16% gross target return from a PE fund (percentage points)

children.text: Now remember the fees. A typical management fee plus a share of profits can absorb most of those last two slices. If what is left is roughly the equity market return, you could have earned that from a Nifty index fund that you can sell tomorrow.

Losses often arrive as defaults or frozen exits

body.title: Responding to the pitch
body.question: A wealth manager says: "Our real estate credit fund had lower volatility than the Nifty over the last five years, so it is the lower-risk option." What is the best response?
options: Agree, because lower volatility always means lower risk
Ask how the fund's holdings are valued and how often, since appraised prices can hide real swings
Pick the Nifty instead, because equities always outperform
Ignore volatility completely, since it tells you nothing about any asset
body.explanation: Volatility is a fair measure for assets with daily market prices, so it is not useless. But for appraised holdings like real estate loans it can badly understate risk. The right move is to find out how the numbers were produced before trusting them.

body.title: Priya's college fund
body.scenario: Priya, 45, lives in Chennai and has saved ₹30 lakh for her daughter's engineering college fees, due in two years. A colleague recommends a real estate debt deal on an online fractional platform: 13% target yield, monthly payouts, a three-year tenure, and "very low volatility." A two-year bank FD or a short-duration debt fund would earn roughly 6 to 7%.
body.prompt: Is the extra return worth it for Priya? Name the specific risks she would be taking that the "low volatility" claim hides, and estimate what the extra return is worth in rupees.
body.modelAnswer:
No. The deal fails before the math even starts.

1. Horizon mismatch: the money is needed in two years, but the tenure is three. Exiting early depends on the platform finding another buyer, possibly at a discount.
2. Default risk: the return depends on one developer paying on time. A delayed project can pause payouts and principal.
3. Concentration: it is a single deal, so one problem affects all ₹30 lakh.
4. Appraisal pricing: "very low volatility" reflects how rarely the deal is revalued, not how safe it is.

The prize: roughly 13% minus 7% gives about 6 percentage points gross, or around ₹1.8 lakh a year before losses, fees and tax. After even modest expected losses and fees, the real pickup is smaller still. The downside is missing a college fee deadline that cannot move. Money with a fixed date belongs in traditional, liquid, low-risk assets. Alternatives are only for money you can genuinely lock away.

points: Higher expected return still requires higher risk. Alternatives do not break that rule; they change what the risk looks like.
Volatility works as a risk measure for assets with daily prices, but appraisal pricing makes alternatives look calmer than they are.
The risks that matter most in alternatives are illiquidity, default, concentration, manager and governance failures, and hidden leverage.
For lending-style alternatives, estimate net return as gross yield minus expected credit loss (PD × LGD) minus fees.
A traditional wrapper chasing alternative returns can carry the same hidden risks, as Franklin Templeton's 2020 debt fund wind-up showed.
Break any target return into market return, illiquidity premium and manager skill, then check how much of the last two survive fees.
